tldr: In humanoid whole-body motion tracking, this research leverages the ultra-fast training speed of off-policy reinforcement learning while using role-sharing among expert models and a dedicated replay mechanism to approach PPO-level tracking accuracy in about 45 minutes.
hero_caption: Overall architecture of LooperMuscle. A semantically structured MoE Actor (policy) adjusts gating weights by body group, an Expert-Aware Critic (value function) aggregates value distributions using those same weights, and Quota-Routed Replay extracts data without bias according to each expert's contribution. Together, they form a single cooperative closed-loop training system.
overview:
To train humanoid robots to imitate human-like whole-body movements in "Whole-Body Tracking (WBT)," on-policy reinforcement learning methods such as PPO (which interact with the environment to collect new data every time the policy updates) have long been the mainstream. However, while PPO is stable, its multi-hour training time has been a major pain point.

Recently, off-policy methods like FastSAC, which store tens of thousands of steps in memory and reuse them, have emerged and solved locomotion tasks in just about 15 minutes. Yet, when applied to whole-body tracking requiring precise coordination across 29 degrees of freedom, tracking accuracy drops significantly compared to PPO—hitting a tough speed-performance tradeoff. A single monolithic neural network simply could not handle two fundamentally different dynamics at once: the lower body, where balance is top priority, and the upper body, which demands expressive motion.

To tackle this challenge, the authors propose "LooperMuscle," a novel learning framework. It tightly couples a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) Actor combining experts across joint groups, a Distributional Critic that directly reflects this division of labor in value estimation, and a quota-routed replay buffer that prevents training from biasing toward only certain experts.

Simulation experiments across 40 diverse human motions showed that LooperMuscle cuts FastSAC's tracking error by 34%, recovering most of the quality that would take PPO about 6 hours in roughly 45 minutes. Furthermore, it successfully achieved zero-shot transfer to a physical Unitree G1 humanoid, proving it can dramatically accelerate practical development cycles.
contributions: Proposed a joint-group-level MoE Actor with anti-collapse regularization, routing experts using different softmax temperatures for the lower and upper body.
Designed an isomorphic Expert-Aware Distributional Critic that reuses the Actor's gating weights to aggregate return distributions across experts.
Introduced a replay mechanism combining quota-based sampling tied to expert contributions with a curriculum that defers difficult transitions.
Reduced tracking error by 34% compared to FastSAC in about 45 minutes of single-GPU training, and successfully tracked dynamic kung-fu motions on a physical Unitree G1 humanoid.

sections.heading: The Speed-Quality Hurdle: Why 15-Minute FastSAC Struggles with Whole-Body Tracking
sections.summary: Combining massively parallel simulators with off-policy RL has dramatically accelerated robot learning, but whole-body motion tracking still lagged far behind PPO in accuracy. Identifying a vicious cycle of monolithic under-capacity, coarse value estimation, and replay imbalance as the root cause, the authors propose LooperMuscle as the solution.
sections.details:
When applying reinforcement learning to physical robots, the speed of iteration—rapidly cycling through training and hardware testing to close the sim-to-real gap—is essential. Recent off-policy methods such as FastSAC demonstrated impressive speed, mastering locomotion on a single GPU in just 15 minutes.

However, when moving to whole-body tracking (WBT) requiring high-precision coordination across 29 joints—such as dance or martial arts—they hit a wall: training was fast, but tracking accuracy fell far short of PPO. The authors identify three interacting causes behind this failure:

- **Limits of a Monolithic MLP**: It forces a compromise between entirely different dynamics—lower-body fall prevention versus upper-body expressive motion.
- **Limits of Scalar Value Functions**: Returning a single scalar for the entire body makes credit assignment difficult: which body parts succeeded and which failed?
- **Pitfalls of Uniform Replay**: Data from body parts that already move well dominate the buffer, burying gradients from struggling, under-trained joints.

LooperMuscle resolves these issues by tightly looping body-group expert models (MoE), an expert-aware distributional critic, and contribution-routed replay. As a result, in roughly 45 minutes—only slightly longer than FastSAC's 15 minutes—it achieves tracking quality approaching that of PPO (around 6 hours).

sections.heading: The Evolution of Humanoid Control: From PPO Dominance to Merging Off-Policy and MoE
sections.summary: Humanoid imitation learning has predominantly relied on monolithic PPO models, though parallel off-policy approaches have recently begun cutting training times. LooperMuscle builds on FastSAC while pioneering the integration of MoE and distributional RL concepts tailored specifically for whole-body tracking.
sections.details:
In physics-simulated character animation and robot motion tracking, PPO-based approaches have been standard ever since DeepMimic. Recent works like BeyondMimic and HOVER also typically rely on a single large neural network to control the entire body.

Meanwhile, to speed up training, researchers explored running Soft Actor-Critic (SAC) and TD3 in parallel environments, showing with FastSAC and FastTD3 that locomotion can be acquired in 15 minutes. However, these methods still use traditional monolithic MLPs, lacking structural extensions needed for complex tasks demanding whole-body coordination.

On another front, Mixture-of-Experts (MoE)—which routes inputs to specialized sub-networks based on expertise—has gained immense popularity in large language models, and robotics has begun showing its utility in large-scale PPO control such as KungfuBot2. LooperMuscle sets itself apart by targeting fast single-task learning, embedding a joint-grouped MoE and an expert-aware distributional value function directly into the FastSAC framework.

sections.heading: How LooperMuscle Works: A Closed-Loop System Driven by Three Mechanisms
sections.summary: The paper introduces a temperature-differentiated MoE Actor splitting the body into upper and lower halves, an isomorphic Expert-Aware Critic matching the expert structure, and Quota-Routed Replay that accounts for expert contribution and sample difficulty. Together, they form a closed training loop that mutually reinforces each component for stable, high-precision learning.
sections.details:
The target platform is a 29-DoF humanoid (Unitree G1). Running at a 50 Hz control frequency, the policy receives proprioceptive observations (joint angles, angular velocities, base orientation, etc.) alongside reference motion signals, outputting target joint positions.

### III-A & III-B: Joint-Group MoE Actor and Anti-Collapse Regularization
Joints are split into two groups—upper body and lower body—and combined across $K$ experts. Key design choices include:
- **Two-Stage Weighting**: In addition to group-level coarse weights ($w_{k,g}$), joint-level scaling factors ($S_{k,j}$) derived from joint ranges are multiplied.
- **Group-Specific Temperatures**: Lower temperatures are set for the lower body (sharpening expert selection to prioritize balance stability), while higher temperatures are used for the upper body (softly blending experts for expressive flexibility).
- **Anti-Collapse Regularization**: To prevent the gating network from collapsing onto a single expert, an auxiliary loss measures the KL divergence between the batch-averaged gating distribution and a uniform distribution, ensuring under-utilized experts still get trained.

### III-C: Isomorphic Expert-Aware Distributional Critic
The critic uses a Distributional Value Function (C51 style) that treats returns as probability distributions, with separate value distribution heads for each of the $K$ experts. By linearly combining these heads using the exact same gating weights computed by the Actor, the critic becomes structurally isomorphic to the actor. This allows precise evaluation of how much each expert's actions contributed to overall value.

### III-D & III-E: Quota-Routed Replay and Closing the Loop
When sampling batches, the replay mechanism enforces fixed quotas so that transitions where each expert had a dominant contribution are reliably represented. Furthermore, difficult transitions with excessively high tracking errors are deferred early in training and gradually phased in via a curriculum schedule. This prevents early optimization collapse while lifting the final performance ceiling.

captions.F4: Data flow of Quota-Routed Replay. Each transition is stored with metadata tracking expert contributions. During minibatch construction, transitions are sampled in a balanced manner according to per-expert quotas and a difficulty-based deferral schedule.

sections.heading: Experimental Results: Reaching 72% of PPO in ~45 Minutes, Excelling on Challenging Fall-and-Recovery Motions
sections.summary: Evaluated across 40 motions from the LAFAN1 dataset against FastSAC-MLP and PPO, LooperMuscle reduced FastSAC's tracking error by 34%. Experts naturally specialized by physical motion phases, and the system successfully reproduced kung-fu sequences on a physical Unitree G1 robot.
sections.details:
Experiments were run on a single NVIDIA RTX 4090D across 4,096 parallel simulation environments, evaluating 40 motions across six categories: walking, running, jumping, dancing, fighting, and fall-and-get-up.

### Speed vs. Accuracy Tradeoff
FastSAC-MLP (~15 minutes of training) had a whole-body position error of 0.153 m, while LooperMuscle (~45 minutes) cut this down by 34.0% to 0.101 m. In terms of normalized reward relative to converged PPO, it reached 72%, nearing 90% on several individual motions. Extending FastSAC's training to 360 minutes plateaued without closing the gap, confirming that the discrepancy stems from network representational capacity rather than raw compute time.

### Performance by Motion Category and Ablations
While the improvement was 26.7% on simple motions like walking, it jumped to 40.6% on highly dynamic, contact-rich fall-and-get-up tasks. This highlights that the division of labor among experts shines most on complex behaviors.
In ablation studies removing one component at a time, dropping the MoE Actor degraded error the most (+51.5%), while removing Quota Replay (+25.7%) and the Deferred schedule (+17.8%) also caused notable drops, verifying the synergy of the proposed modules.

### Expert Specialization and Hardware Deployment
t-SNE feature visualizations (Figure F5) revealed that experts formed clear clusters not by motion category, but by physical control modes such as stance and swing phases. Additionally, deploying a model retrained with a 154-dimensional interface relying solely on onboard sensors onto the physical Unitree G1 (Figure F7) confirmed smooth tracking of kicking and kung-fu sequences without falling.

captions.F5: t-SNE visualization of penultimate-layer representations colored by dominant Expert ID. Experts form distinct clusters, showing that specialization emerges along mechanical modes (such as support leg transitions) rather than high-level motion types.
captions.F7: Hardware whole-body tracking experiments on the Unitree G1 humanoid performing kung-fu motions. Running at 50 Hz using only a 154-dimensional onboard-estimable observation interface, the robot executes a continuous sequence from dynamic kicks to stable landings and transitions.

sections.heading: Conclusion and Outlook: How Fast Iteration Shapes the Future of Humanoid Control
sections.summary: LooperMuscle is a practical framework that pairs the training speed of off-policy RL with the high tracking accuracy of PPO. It also outlines clear directions for future improvements, such as bridging observation gaps between simulation and hardware and automating hyperparameter tuning.
sections.details:
By coupling a joint-grouped MoE, an isomorphic distributional critic, and contribution-routed replay, this work significantly advances the speed-quality tradeoff in humanoid whole-body tracking. Slashing training time from 6 hours down to 45 minutes provides immense practical value by drastically accelerating the trial-and-error loop in sim-to-real workflows.

The paper highlights three key areas for future work:
- **Unifying Observation Interfaces**: Benchmark evaluations currently rely on privileged simulation data (such as global positions), requiring models to be retrained exclusively with onboard sensor data for hardware deployment. Future work should unify all benchmarks under realistic onboard observation spaces.
- **Fair Capacity Comparisons**: Evaluating against scaled-up MLPs with matched parameter counts will help further isolate the architectural advantages of MoE.
- **Automating Architectural Design**: Hyperparameters such as the number of experts ($K=4$) and gating temperatures were kept fixed; developing mechanisms to adapt these dynamically remains an exciting avenue.

takeaways: The tracking performance drop in off-policy RL (FastSAC) was not due to a lack of training time, but rather the representational bottleneck of a monolithic MLP.

In humanoid whole-body control, an MoE design using differentiated gating temperatures across body groups—low temperature for lower-body stability, high temperature for upper-body expressiveness—proves remarkably effective.

The closed-loop architectural harmony—keeping the Actor's MoE and Critic's value distribution structures isomorphic while preventing expert starvation via replay routing—is what truly drives performance gains.
limitations: Quantitative benchmark evaluations rely on privileged simulation data (such as global coordinates), requiring the policy to be retrained from scratch with onboard sensor inputs before real-world deployment.

Hyperparameters such as the number of experts ($K=4$) and group partitions ($G=2$) are heuristically fixed, and strict comparisons against parameter-matched monolithic MLPs have not yet been conducted.
